messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Cybersecurity Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Vignette:
Leilani Fono is a 65-year-old widowed woman of Samoan descent who works as a cybersecurity analyst for a mid-sized financial services firm in Phoenix, Arizona. She was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to her primary care physician that she had not slept through the night in nearly eight months. Her PCL-5 score of 80 places her symptoms in the severe range, and what emerged across the intake and early sessions was a clinical picture of considerable complexity and suffering.

Eight months ago, Leilani was driving home from a late shift when a commercial delivery truck ran a red light and struck her vehicle on the driver's side at highway speed. The impact crushed the door inward, trapping her for nearly forty minutes before emergency services could free her. She sustained fractures to her left shoulder, two ribs, and her pelvis. What she has described most vividly, however, is not the pain but the smell — engine fluid and something burning, filling the cabin while she could not move. She remembers the specific quality of the afternoon light and the image of the truck's grille filling her window in the half-second before impact, an image she says is still "just there, behind my eyes" whenever she is not actively occupied with something else. In the weeks following her discharge from hospital, she began to notice that the memory did not behave the way she expected memory to behave. It arrived not as a recollection but as a sensory event — the smell of oil or exhaust on a colleague's jacket could return her, without warning, to that crushed cabin, and with it came the same pressure across her pelvis and ribs that she had felt pinned inside the car.

Leilani had come to believe, with quiet but firm conviction, that her body was no longer something she could rely on. She had been healthy and physically capable her entire adult life, and the accident had revealed, in her understanding, that this was always an illusion. She was also certain that the accident was deeply unjust — the truck driver had received only a minor citation, the company had not been held accountable, and no one, she felt, had acknowledged what had actually been taken from her. This sense of unresolved wrong had become a persistent presence in her thinking. She found herself returning again and again to the question of why this had happened to her specifically — running through the timeline of that evening, the route she had chosen, whether a different decision at any point might have changed the outcome. These cycles of thought occupied her during the hours she was meant to be sleeping.

Sleep had become its own ordeal. Leilani did not feel safe lying in the dark, and she had developed a habit of waking at intervals through the night to check the locks, the windows, and the street outside. Darkness carried a quality of exposure and vulnerability that daylight did not, and she could not fully account for this except to say that it felt true in a way that reasoning could not touch. She had taken to leaving a light on in the hallway and the television running at low volume, not for comfort exactly, but because silence and darkness were conditions she could no longer tolerate.

At work, the consequences had become impossible to ignore. Leilani's role required sustained analytical focus and engagement with complex threat-monitoring systems — a bitter irony she had not missed. A colleague who worked on a lower floor sometimes returned from the parking garage smelling of engine exhaust, and on two occasions Leilani had left the open-plan office floor abruptly without explanation. She had begun declining team lunches and after-work events, not because she disliked her colleagues but because she had concluded that emotional neutrality was the safest state available to her — that allowing herself to feel anything, even pleasure, created a kind of opening she was not willing to risk. Her manager had asked, gently, whether she was all right. Leilani had said yes. What frightened her most about that question was the feeling that the answer was visible on her face regardless of what she said — that whatever had happened to her had marked her in some way others could read.

What finally brought her to seek help was a performance review in which her attention and responsiveness were noted as concerns. Leilani had spent thirty years building a professional identity grounded in precision and reliability. Losing that, she said in the first session, was something she could not accept. What she hoped for, she added after a long pause, was to feel like herself again. What she feared was that the self she remembered no longer existed to return to.
